newsitem.title: USA: Clinton said set to name ex-aide as chief of staff.
newsitem.headline: Clinton said set to name ex-aide as chief of staff.

text.p: President Bill Clinton plans to name Erskine Bowles, a North Carolina investment banker and former top White House official, as his new chief of staff, an administration official said on Friday.
The official, who declined to be identified, said Clinton was likely to announce the appointment at a 3 p.m. EST (2000 GMT) news conference on Friday.

Bowles, 51, would replace Leon Panetta, a former congressman who has won high marks as Clinton's chief of staff. He has made no secret of his desire to leave the White House and was believed to be considering making a run for governor of his home state, California, in 1998.

Bowles previously served Clinton in several jobs, most recently as deputy chief of staff at the White House. He left in December 1995 to return to private life in North Carolina and join an investment firm.
Although there are almost always some changes in top level positions during U.S. presidential transitions, the prospective shakeup of Clinton's team is unusually sweeping.

Besides Panetta's departure, six Cabinet secretaries have made known their plans to leave since Clinton won re-election on Tuesday. The first to make it official and public was Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who announced his resignation on Thursday effective in January and was saluted by Clinton at a special White House ceremony.

Clinton hinted then that he wanted to name a Republican to the Cabinet, but in the contest for secretary of state, at least, that seemed less likely as officials said former Sen. George Mitchell, a Democrat, looked to be the top candidate.
But officials have said Clinton has been working hardest to find a replacement for the chief of staff, the most powerful job in the White House other than the president's.

The chief of staff essentially controls access to the president himself and sets much of his agenda. The president in turn counts on him to get his orders carried out quickly and effectively and to keep staff operations humming smoothly.
Having raised money for Clinton in the South during his 1992 campaign, Bowles was brought to Washington after that election to run the Small Business Admistration in 1993-94.

He acquired a reputation as a Clinton loyalist at the SBA, and gained the president's ear as a member of the National Economic Council, the White House team that coordinates the administration's economic policy. He was a deputy White House chief of staff in 1995.
That year, Bowles went before the Senate Whitewater Committee to answer questions about a small business loan made to former Clinton business partner Susan McDougal.
McDougal was jailed this year for refusing to testify about Clinton's role in the complex web of bank and real estate dealings known as Whitewater.

Bowles gave investigators little specific information when asked about accusations that the White House got confidential information from the SBA about Clinton's chief Whitewater accuser, former Arkansas municipal judge David Hale.
Clinton used Bowles for delicate political assignments even after his departure from the White House and often sought him out as a golf partner.

In August, the president asked him to undertake the sensitive task of speaking to top campaign strategist Dick Morris after news reports surfaced that Morris had engaged in a year-long relationship with a prostitute.
After a talk with Bowles, Morris resigned on the final day of the Democratic National Convention, shortly before Clinton made his speech accepting the party's presidential nomination.
Born August 8, 1945, Bowles worked as an investment banker in New York but left in 1975 to co-found a bank, Hollowell Conner & Co, in his native North Carolina.
Currently a partner in Carousel Capital Co. in Charlotte, North Carolina, Bowles is married and has three children.
